citations.quote: For the Lebesgue branches (a) and (b) assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the exact measure interface ([[def-countable-choice]]); the finite sums in branch (c) are defined and computed without Choice. Let the laboratory region, its chart, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\delta_{ij}$ be the Kronecker symbol in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame, with $|y|$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This definition assigns **source moments** to a static charge distribution in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (d) and (e). Three branches are declared. (a) [Absolutely continuous branch] Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and vanish $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $\overline B_a(0)=\{y:|y|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The **total charge** $Q$, the **dipole moment** $p$, the **degree-$l$ Cartesian moments** $M_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and the **traceless quadrupole** $Q_{ij}$ are $$Q:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p_i:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_i\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\ (l\ge1),$$ $$M^{(0)}:=Q,\qquad M_i:=p_i,\qquad Q_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$ with $l\ge1$ and indices in $\{1,2,3\}$; units are C for $Q$, C m for $p$, C m$^l$ for the degree-$l$ Cartesian moment and C m$^2$ for $Q_{ij}$, and all integrals are in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Each integral is absolutely convergent: since $\rho=0$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$, and the maps $y\mapsto y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}$ and $y\mapsto 3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}$ are bounded $\lambda_3$-a.e. on that ball by $a^l$ and by $4a^2$ respectively, the integrands are dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by $a^l|\rho|$ and $4a^2|\rho|$, which lie in $L^1$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]])

For the Lebesgue branches (a) and (b) assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the exact measure interface ([[def-countable-choice]]); the finite sums in branch (c) are defined and computed without Choice. Let the laboratory region, its chart, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\delta_{ij}$ be the Kronecker symbol in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame, with $|y|$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This definition assigns **source moments** to a static charge distribution in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (d) and (e). Three branches are declared. (a) [Absolutely continuous branch] Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and vanish $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $\overline B_a(0)=\{y:|y|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The **total charge** $Q$, the **dipole moment** $p$, the **degree-$l$ Cartesian moments** $M_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and the **traceless quadrupole** $Q_{ij}$ are $$Q:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p_i:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_i\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\ (l\ge1),$$ $$M^{(0)}:=Q,\qquad M_i:=p_i,\qquad Q_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$ with $l\ge1$ and indices in $\{1,2,3\}$; units are C for $Q$, C m for $p$, C m$^l$ for the degree-$l$ Cartesian moment and C m$^2$ for $Q_{ij}$, and all integrals are in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Each integral is absolutely convergent: since $\rho=0$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$, and the maps $y\mapsto y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}$ and $y\mapsto 3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}$ are bounded $\lambda_3$-a.e. on that ball by $a^l$ and by $4a^2$ respectively, the integrands are dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by $a^l|\rho|$ and $4a^2|\rho|$, which lie in $L^1$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). The traceless quadrupole is traceless, $$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$ because $\sum_{i=1}^3(3y_i^2-|y|^2)=0$ pointwise, and summing the three integrable functions $3y_i^2\rho-|y|^2\rho$ and applying finite linearity of the integral on $L^1$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]) evaluates the sum as the integral of the pointwise-zero function; replacing $\rho$ by an equal $\lambda_3$-a.e. density changes no moment ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). (b) [General locally integrable branch] If instead $\rho\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ is real and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^l|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)<\infty$ for a given integer $l\ge0$, then the degree-$l$ Cartesian moments of the same formula are absolutely convergent and defined; if the absolute weighted moment $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^L|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)$ is finite for some real $L\ge0$, then every integer Cartesian degree $0\le l\le L$ is defined, and in particular $Q=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3$ is absolutely convergent, so that $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ is a conclusion of this branch and not an added hypothesis. Here $\rho$ is restricted to the closed unit ball, where it is integrable by local integrability, and outside it $|y|^l\le|y|^L$; splitting the nonnegative integral over these two measurable sets and applying monotonicity and additivity of the integral gives $\int|y|^l|\rho|\le\int_{\overline B_1(0)}|\rho|+\int_{\{|y|>1\}}|y|^L|\rho|<\infty$ ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-metric-ball]]). The convention $|y|^0=1$ includes the origin, no compact support and no $L^1$-membership is assumed in this branch, and Cartesian monomials of degree $l$ have modulus at most $|y|^l$, so all lower moments, including $Q$, exist together with the degree-$l$ moment. (c) [Finite system of stationary point charges] Let $N\ge0$, let $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\mathbb R^3$ and let $q_1,\dots,q_N\in\mathbb R$ be charge parameters ([[def-em-sources]] (a)), read as the stationary point charges $q_k\delta_{x_k}$ in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e); for $N=0$ the lists are empty and every sum below is the empty sum $0$. Define $$Q:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k,\qquad p:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_kx_k,\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\,x_{k,i_1}\cdots x_{k,i_l}\ (l\ge1),\qquad M^{(0)}:=Q,$$ $$Q_{ij}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\bigl(3x_{k,i}x_{k,j}-|x_k|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr),$$ finite sums in the sense of [[def-finite-sum]] ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]); again $$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$ by finite distributivity

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is complex-linear on it: $$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f,g\in L^1(\mu)$. Then the following are equivalent: 1. $f=g$ almost everywhere; 2. for every measurable $A$, $$\int_A f\,d\mu=\int_A g\,d\mu.$$ For integrable real or complex $h$, the notation in condition 2 means $\int_A h\,d\mu:=\int h\chi_A\,d\mu$; the product is integrable because $|h\chi_A|\le|h|$.
If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then $$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$
Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$. 1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$. 2

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$ ([[def-nat-addition]]). Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for $a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]])

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then: 1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$. 2

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set, and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so $$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$ is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$, a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations ([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is)

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then: 1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.** $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$ with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$. 2

**Clause 1 is about an arbitrary norm; clauses 2 to 4 are about $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $n \ge 1$.** 1. **Finite and reverse triangle inequalities.** Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ and $N$ a norm on it ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For every $p \in \mathbb{N}$ and every list $u : p \to V$ ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]), $$N\Bigl(\sum_{j<p} u_j\Bigr) \;\le\; \sum_{j<p} N(u_j),$$ and for all $u, w \in V$, $$\bigl|N(u) - N(w)\bigr| \;\le\; N(u - w).$$ Now let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ carry the norms of [[def-p-norms-on-rn]] and write $\iota$ for the canonical natural ([[def-canonical-natural]]). 2
Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define $$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$ $B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the **sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$

derivations.claim: Establish that every integral in the definition of the $b$-moments is absolutely convergent. For $\lambda_3$-a.e. $y$ outside $\overline B_a(0)$ the integrands vanish, and for $y\in\overline B_a(0)$ one has $|y|\le a$ by [F9], so $|(y-b)_{i_1}\cdots(y-b)_{i_l}|\le(|y|+|b|)^l\le(a+|b|)^l$ and $|3(y-b)_i(y-b)_j-|y-b|^2\delta_{ij}|\le3|y-b|^2+|y-b|^2\le4(a+|b|)^2$ by [F7]; hence each integrand is bounded $\lambda_3$-a.e. on the support by a finite constant times $|\rho|\in L^1$, and the triangle and monotonicity rules [F5] give absolute convergence.

Prove the polynomial expansion identity: for every $l\ge0$, all indices $i_1,\dots,i_l\in\{1,2,3\}$ and every $y\in\mathbb R^3$, $\prod_{r=1}^l(y-b)_{i_r}=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\dots,l\}}(-1)^{|S|}\bigl(\prod_{r\in S}b_{i_r}\bigr)\bigl(\prod_{r\in S^{c}}y_{i_r}\bigr)$, where empty products are $1$ and $S^{c}=\{1,\dots,l\}\setminus S$. The case $l=0$ is $1=1$, the unique subset being $S=\emptyset$; for $l\ge1$ write the product as $\bigl(\prod_{r=1}^{l-1}(y-b)_{i_r}\bigr)(y_{i_l}-b_{i_l})$, apply the induction hypothesis to the first factor and distribute: the subsets $S$ of $\{1,\dots,l-1\}$ that avoid $l$ and the subsets to which $l$ is adjoined are in bijection and reindex the same finite sum, giving the displayed identity.

In the density branch, substitute step 1.2 into the definition of $M^{(b)}_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and integrate term by term. Each summand is a real constant $(-1)^{|S|}\prod_{r\in S}b_{i_r}$ times the $L^1$ function $y\mapsto(\prod_{r\in S^{c}}y_{i_r})\rho(y)$, which is dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by $|b|^{|S|}a^{l-|S|}|\rho|$ by [F1] and [F7]; finite linearity [F3] and the a.e. support convention [F4] therefore give $M^{(b)}_{i_1\dots i_l}=\sum_{S}(-1)^{|S|}\bigl(\prod_{r\in S}b_{i_r}\bigr)M_{S^{c}}$ with $M_{\emptyset}:=Q$. Specialising to $l=0$ gives $Q^{(b)}=Q$, which is (a). Specialising to $l=1$ gives $p^{(b)}_i=p_i-b_iQ$, which is (b): if $Q=0$ then $p^{(b)}=p$ for every $b$; conversely, if $p^{(b)}=p$ for every $b\in\mathbb R^3$, then $Qb=0$ for every $b$, and taking $b=e_1$ gives $Qe_1=0$, whose first coordinate is $Q$, so $Q=0$, and the dipole moment is independent of the reference point exactly when $Q=0$.

Evaluate the $l=2$ instance of step 2.1: $M^{(b)}_{ij}=M_{ij}-b_ip_j-b_jp_i+b_ib_jQ$. Summing over $i=j$ and using finite linearity [F3] gives $\sum_{k=1}^3M^{(b)}_{kk}=\sum_{k=1}^3M_{kk}-2b\cdot p+|b|^2Q$, where $b\cdot p=\sum_kb_kp_k$ is the Euclidean inner product [F7].

Compute the traceless quadrupole about $b$. By [F1], $Q^{(b)}_{ij}=3M^{(b)}_{ij}-\delta_{ij}\sum_kM^{(b)}_{kk}$ and $Q_{ij}=3M_{ij}-\delta_{ij}\sum_kM_{kk}$, so substituting step 3.1 into the first identity gives $Q^{(b)}_{ij}=Q_{ij}-3(b_ip_j+b_jp_i)+2(b\cdot p)\delta_{ij}+(3b_ib_j-|b|^2\delta_{ij})Q$, which is the displayed identity of (d); every step is a finite algebraic rearrangement [F3].

If $Q=0$ and $p=0$, the $b$-dependent terms of step 4.1 vanish, so every quadrupole component is reference-point independent. Conversely, suppose $Q^{(b)}_{ij}=Q_{ij}$ for all $b,i,j$. The $11$ components of step 4.1 at $b=e_1$ and $b=-e_1$ give $-4p_1+2Q=0$ and $4p_1+2Q=0$; adding gives $Q=0$. With $Q=0$, the $ii$ component at $b=e_i$ is $-4p_i=0$ for each $i$, hence $p=0$. This proves the equivalence in (d).

Repeat the argument in the finite point-charge branch and complete the choice accounting. The same expansion identity of step 1.2 is substituted into the finite sums of [F2]; finite distributivity, reindexing and the empty-sum convention [F6] produce the identical identities (a)-(d) with sums in place of integrals, without any convergence hypothesis, and the case $N=0$ makes both sides $0$ at every step. The identities are therefore choice-free in this branch, while the density branch used only the declared Countable Choice of the measure interface.

Combine the branches and record the scope. Replacing $\rho$ by an equal $\lambda_3$-a.e. density leaves every $b$-moment unchanged by [F4], so (a)-(d) hold as stated for the declared representatives; the density branch is established in steps 2.1, 4.1 and 5.1, the finite-point branch in step 6.1, and the identities are those of the source moments of [[def-em-electric-moments]] about the chart origin, the reference point $b$ being a choice of coordinate origin only; no field, force or dynamical content is asserted, which is clause (e).

citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. For a measurable compactly supported $f$, define $$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$$ at each $x$ where the integral is absolutely finite

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the cited Lebesgue, polar, Newtonian and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Work in $\mathbb R^3$ with its Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]) and the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$. Let $\Phi$ be the $n=3$ fundamental solution of $-\Delta$ of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], normalised by $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$; then $\omega_2=4\pi$ and $$\Phi(z)=\frac{1}{4\pi|z|}\qquad(z\ne0)$$ ([[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]])

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the cited Lebesgue, polar, Newtonian and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Work in $\mathbb R^3$ with its Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]) and the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$. Let $\Phi$ be the $n=3$ fundamental solution of $-\Delta$ of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], normalised by $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$; then $\omega_2=4\pi$ and $$\Phi(z)=\frac{1}{4\pi|z|}\qquad(z\ne0)$$ ([[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]). Let $Nf$ be the Newtonian potential of [[def-newtonian-potential]]. (a) [Smooth compact sources] Let $\rho:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ with compact support contained in $\overline B_R$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-metric-ball]]), put $\varphi:=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho$ and $E:=-\nabla\varphi$. Then $\varphi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ ([[thm-newtonian-potential-for-holder-data-is-classical]]), and pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$ $$-\Delta\varphi=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0$$ with the operators of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Moreover, with $Q:=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3$, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ the absolutely convergent Coulomb integral representation holds, and its far-field bound holds for $|x|>2R$, $$E(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{x-y}{|x-y|^3}\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad |E(x)|\le\frac{\| \rho\|_1}{\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2}\quad(|x|>2R),$$ and for $|x|>\max(2R,1)$ the potential obeys the decay bound $|\varphi(x)|\le\bigl(|Q|/(4\pi)+R\|\rho\|_1/\pi\bigr)/(\varepsilon_0|x|)$ ([[lem-em-newtonian-far-field-gradient]], [[thm-decay-of-the-newtonian-potential-of-compactly-supported-data]]). The pair $(E,0,\rho,0)$ therefore realises the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with source $\rho$, and $E$ is the field of the localised Newtonian potential. (b) [Uniqueness with vanishing at infinity] If $\psi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfies $-\Delta\psi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$ and $\lim_{|x|\to\infty}\psi(x)=0$, then $\psi=\varphi$ ([[thm-weak-maximum-principle-for-the-laplacian]]). In particular, among $C^2$ solutions of the Poisson equation of a compactly supported $C^1$ source decaying at infinity, the localised Newtonian potential is the unique one. Let the laboratory region, its chart, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\delta_{ij}$ be the Kronecker symbol in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame, with $|y|$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This definition assigns **source moments** to a static charge distribution in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (d) and (e). Three branches are declared.

(a) [Absolutely continuous branch] Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and vanish $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $\overline B_a(0)=\{y:|y|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The **total charge** $Q$, the **dipole moment** $p$, the **degree-$l$ Cartesian moments** $M_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and the **traceless quadrupole** $Q_{ij}$ are

$$Q:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p_i:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_i\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\ (l\ge1),$$

$$M^{(0)}:=Q,\qquad M_i:=p_i,\qquad Q_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$

with $l\ge1$ and indices in $\{1,2,3\}$; units are C for $Q$, C m for $p$, C m$^l$ for the degree-$l$ Cartesian moment and C m$^2$ for $Q_{ij}$, and all integrals are in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Each integral is absolutely convergent: since $\rho=0$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$, and the maps $y\mapsto y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}$ and $y\mapsto 3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}$ are bounded $\lambda_3$-a.e. on that ball by $a^l$ and by $4a^2$ respectively, the integrands are dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by $a^l|\rho|$ and $4a^2|\rho|$, which lie in $L^1$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). The traceless quadrupole is traceless,

$$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$

because $\sum_{i=1}^3(3y_i^2-|y|^2)=0$ pointwise, and summing the three integrable functions $3y_i^2\rho-|y|^2\rho$ and applying finite linearity of the integral on $L^1$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]) evaluates the sum as the integral of the pointwise-zero function; replacing $\rho$ by an equal $\lambda_3$-a.e. density changes no moment ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]).

(c) [Finite system of stationary point charges] Let $N\ge0$, let $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\mathbb R^3$ and let $q_1,\dots,q_N\in\mathbb R$ be charge parameters ([[def-em-sources]] (a)), read as the stationary point charges $q_k\delta_{x_k}$ in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e); for $N=0$ the lists are empty and every sum below is the empty sum $0$. Define

$$Q:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k,\qquad p:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_kx_k,\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\,x_{k,i_1}\cdots x_{k,i_l}\ (l\ge1),\qquad M^{(0)}:=Q,$$

$$Q_{ij}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\bigl(3x_{k,i}x_{k,j}-|x_k|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr),$$

finite sums in the sense of [[def-finite-sum]] ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]); again

$$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$

by finite distributivity. The points need not be distinct; charges at a common point add in every sum.

(d) [Reference point and scope] Every moment of (a)-(c) is computed about the chart origin of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; this origin is part of the definition. These are source moments of a prescribed static distribution, not momenta, rest masses, intrinsic spins, self-energies or dynamical quantities, and no field, force, equation of motion, equilibrium or empirical claim is made here; the static regime in which the source is read is the adopted idealisation of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (f). Every Cartesian degree $l$ in this definition is a nonnegative integer (the number of Cartesian indices); only the absolute weighted exponent $L$ in (b) may be any nonnegative real number.

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. For a measurable compactly supported
$f$, define
$$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$$
at each $x$ where the integral is absolutely finite. Whenever this integral
is finite almost everywhere, $Nf$ also denotes its almost-everywhere class.
The following items establish everywhere convergence for bounded compact data
and almost-everywhere convergence for compact $L^1$ data; the definition itself
makes no unconditional convergence claim.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the cited Lebesgue, polar, Newtonian and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]).
Work in $\mathbb R^3$ with its Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]) and the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$.
Let $\Phi$ be the $n=3$ fundamental solution of $-\Delta$ of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], normalised by $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$; then $\omega_2=4\pi$ and
$$\Phi(z)=\frac{1}{4\pi|z|}\qquad(z\ne0)$$
([[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]).
Let $Nf$ be the Newtonian potential of [[def-newtonian-potential]].

(a) [Smooth compact sources] Let $\rho:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ with compact support contained in $\overline B_R$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-metric-ball]]), put $\varphi:=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho$ and $E:=-\nabla\varphi$.
Then $\varphi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ ([[thm-newtonian-potential-for-holder-data-is-classical]]), and pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$
$$-\Delta\varphi=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0$$
with the operators of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]].
Moreover, with $Q:=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3$, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ the absolutely convergent Coulomb integral representation holds, and its far-field bound holds for $|x|>2R$,
$$E(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{x-y}{|x-y|^3}\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad |E(x)|\le\frac{\| \rho\|_1}{\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2}\quad(|x|>2R),$$
and for $|x|>\max(2R,1)$ the potential obeys the decay bound $|\varphi(x)|\le\bigl(|Q|/(4\pi)+R\|\rho\|_1/\pi\bigr)/(\varepsilon_0|x|)$ ([[lem-em-newtonian-far-field-gradient]], [[thm-decay-of-the-newtonian-potential-of-compactly-supported-data]]).
The pair $(E,0,\rho,0)$ therefore realises the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with source $\rho$, and $E$ is the field of the localised Newtonian potential.

(b) [Uniqueness with vanishing at infinity] If $\psi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfies $-\Delta\psi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$ and $\lim_{|x|\to\infty}\psi(x)=0$, then $\psi=\varphi$ ([[thm-weak-maximum-principle-for-the-laplacian]]).
In particular, among $C^2$ solutions of the Poisson equation of a compactly supported $C^1$ source decaying at infinity, the localised Newtonian potential is the unique one.

(c) [Compactly supported $L^1$ sources] If instead $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ is real, measurable and compactly supported, then $N\rho$ is finite $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere, belongs to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$, is $C^\infty$ and harmonic off the support of $\rho$, and its regular distribution satisfies
$$-\Delta T_{\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho}=T_{\rho/\varepsilon_0}\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$$
([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]], scaled by $\varepsilon_0^{-1}$; [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(d) [Point charge] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ and $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and define, with arbitrary values at $x_0$,
$$\varphi_q(x):=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|},\qquad E_q(x):=\frac{q\,(x-x_0)}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|^3}\qquad(x\ne x_0).$$
Then $\varphi_q\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $E_q$ is locally integrable and $C^\infty$ off $x_0$, $E_q=-\nabla\varphi_q$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{x_0\}$, and, with $T_{\varphi_q}$ the regular distribution of $\varphi_q$ and $\operatorname{div}E_q:=\sum_i\partial_iT_{E_{q,i}}$, $\operatorname{curl}E_q:=(\partial_2T_{E_{q,3}}-\partial_3T_{E_{q,2}},\ \partial_3T_{E_{q,1}}-\partial_1T_{E_{q,3}},\ \partial_1T_{E_{q,2}}-\partial_2T_{E_{q,1}})$,
$$-\Delta T_{\varphi_q}=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\delta_{x_0},\qquad \operatorname{div}E_q=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\delta_{x_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}E_q=0\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$$
([[thm-minus-laplacian-of-the-fundamental-solution-is-dirac]] for the first identity, [[lem-em-distributional-gradient-smooth-off-a-point]] for the passage from the potential to the field, [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]).
The distribution $q\delta_{x_0}$ is the fixed-time reading of the stationary point charge of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with charge parameter $q$ and constant trajectory $z\equiv x_0$ ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](e)); so the pair $(E_q,0)$ satisfies the distributional pure electrostatic equations with that point source.
This is an idealised point-source model: no claim of uniqueness for the point source, no self-force and no statement about the field at $x_0$ itself is made.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity

$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units, constants and symbols of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and let $(\rho,J)$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$, all of class $C^1$ (with every additional derivative appearing below existing and continuous); $\partial_t$ is the partial time derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

(a) [Static regime] The **static (time-independent) electromagnetic regime** on $\Omega\times I$ is the requirement
$$\partial_tE=0,\qquad\partial_tB=0,\qquad\partial_t\rho=0,\qquad\partial_tJ=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$

(b) [Pure electrostatics] The **pure electrostatic regime** is the static regime together with $J=0$ and $B=0$ on $\Omega\times I$.

(c) [Reduced equations] If the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds in the static regime, then the four Maxwell equations reduce to
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$$
pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied at each fixed time; in the pure electrostatic regime the reduction is exactly the pair $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$.

(d) [Fixed-time reading] In the static regime $E,B,\rho,J$ do not depend on $t$, so each is the pullback along $(y,t)\mapsto y$ of a single map on $\Omega$; this fixed-time reading (the spatial field or source) is the object analysed by the electrostatic statements of this page, and no other time dependence is introduced. The equations of (c) are equations between those spatial maps.

(e) [Static-to-distributional reading] Let fields $E,B$ and volume densities $\rho,J$ be locally integrable and time independent on $\Omega\times I$, and let $\Omega$ be open. Then, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the cited measure and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]), the weak equations of the solution predicate of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e) for these time-independent objects hold if and only if the four spatial equations $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$; the passage between them is the integration in $t$ of the pairings against $C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ tests, justified by [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] after identifying fields and densities with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). In particular a **stationary point charge** at $x_0\in\Omega$ with charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ is the point source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with constant trajectory $z(t)\equiv x_0$, whose pairing is $\psi\mapsto q\int_I\psi(x_0,t)\,dt$ and whose fixed-time reading is the spatial point source $\eta\mapsto q\eta(x_0)$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]).

(f) [Conventions and scope] The regime is imposed in the one inertial frame of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; no claim is made that time independence survives a change of inertial description, and where a frame change is used the transformed fields must be rechecked. The static regime is an adopted idealization, not a dynamical stability theorem: static charged matter requires external support or an adopted equilibrium model. No equation is asserted here for singular sources beyond the dictionary of (e), and no empirical claim is made.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mathcal P_l$ denote the real vector space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $l$ on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-homogeneous-polynomial-and-homogeneous-ideal]], [[def-monomials-multidegree-and-total-degree]]), $H_l=\ker(\Delta:\mathcal P_l\to\mathcal P_{l-2})$ with $\mathcal P_k=\{0\}$ for $k<0$, and let spherical harmonics of degree $l$ be the restrictions of $H_l$ to $S^2$, with unnormalised surface measure $d\Omega$ of total mass $4\pi$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]). Then $\mathcal P_l=H_l\oplus|x|^2\mathcal P_{l-2}$, $\dim H_l=2l+1$, harmonics of distinct degree are orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$, and the union over $l$ of the spaces of spherical harmonics admits a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). For any real orthonormal basis $Y_{lm}$, $m=1,\dots,2l+1$, of degree-$l$ harmonics the addition theorem holds:

$$\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')=\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}P_l(n\cdot n'),$$

where $P_l$ is the Legendre polynomial of the convergent zonal kernel lemma ([[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]). The Laplacian is the Euclidean one ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). This supplies the harmonic decomposition, orthogonality, completeness and exact addition kernel; it does not assert higher boundary regularity. The purely polynomial decomposition and finite dimension identities use no Choice; the surface/$L^2$/completeness claims retain the stated Countable Choice.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\lambda_3)$ be a real or complex valued Lebesgue integrable function on $\mathbb R^3$ that vanishes $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $B_a:=\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2\le a\}$ ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], [[def-metric-ball]]). Put

$$Q:=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p:=\int y\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3\in\mathbb C^3,\qquad \lVert\rho\rVert_1:=\int\lvert\rho\rvert\,d\lambda_3,$$

the vector $p$ being defined by $p_k:=\int y_k\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)$ for the canonical coordinates $k<3$, namely $k\in\{0,1,2\}$, and $\langle p,x\rangle:=\sum_{k<3}p_kx_k$ being the complex-bilinear coordinate contraction, with no complex conjugation, which agrees with the real Euclidean pairing when $p$ is real; if $\rho$ is real-valued then $Q$ is real and $p\in\mathbb R^3$, while $R(x)$ below is real in that case and complex in general. Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ with $r:=\lVert x\rVert_2\ge2a>0$,

$$\int\frac{\rho(y)}{\lVert x-y\rVert_2}\,d\lambda_3(y)=\frac Qr+\frac{\langle p,x\rangle}{r^3}+R(x),\qquad R(x):=\int_{B_a}\rho(y)\Bigl(\frac1{\lVert x-y\rVert_2}-\frac1r-\frac{\langle x,y\rangle}{r^3}\Bigr)d\lambda_3(y),$$

and the remainder satisfies the explicit bound

$$\lvert R(x)\rvert\le\frac{16\,a^2\,\lVert\rho\rVert_1}{r^3}.$$

In the all-space kernel integral define $K_x(y)=\lVert x-y\rVert_2^{-1}$ for $y\ne x$ and $K_x(x)=0$, so its integrand means $\rho K_x$ and is an everywhere-defined measurable function. This convention cannot affect the integral: $x\notin B_a$ and the density vanishes almost everywhere outside $B_a$. All integrals are Lebesgue integrals; the closed ball $B_a$ is Borel and $\chi_{B_a}\rho$ is integrable. The constant $16$ is permissible but not sharp, and $Q$, $p$ and $\lVert\rho\rVert_1$ are finite. No derivative of the remainder in $x$ is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ vanish outside $\overline B_a(0)$. Use the complete orthonormal basis $\{Y_{lm}\}$ of real spherical harmonics on $S^2$ with unnormalised surface measure $d\sigma$ of total mass $4\pi$ and the addition theorem of [[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]], and the Legendre generating kernel and its compact remainder bound from [[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]. Write $x=rn$, $r=|x|$, $n\in S^2$. Then:

(a) **Exterior multipole expansion.** For every $x$ with $|x|>a$, $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy=\sum_{l=0}^\infty\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}\frac{Y_{lm}(n)}{r^{l+1}}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^lY_{lm}(y/|y|)\rho(y)\,dy,$$ the series converging absolutely and uniformly on $\{|x|\ge r_0\}$ for every $r_0>a$, with tail after degree $N$ bounded by $\|\rho\|_1\,a^{N+1}/(r_0^{N+2}(1-a/r_0))$; for every fixed $r>a$, the degree-$l$ term is the $L^2(S^2,d\sigma)$ angular projection of $n\mapsto F_r(n):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}|rn-y|^{-1}\rho(y)\,dy$ onto the degree-$l$ harmonics. This function is continuous and bounded by $\|\rho\|_1/(r-a)$, so it is in $L^2(S^2)$; no sphere trace or $L^2$ property of the volume density $\rho$ is asserted. The degree-zero and degree-one terms are the Coulomb and dipole terms with the explicit remainder bound of [[lem-em-coulomb-dipole-remainder]] ($Q=\int\rho$, $p=\int y\rho(y)\,dy$, $|R(x)|\le16a^2\|\rho\|_1/|x|^3$ for $|x|\ge2a$).

(b) **Termwise differentiation.** On every compact $K$ with $\inf_K|x|>a$ the series may be differentiated termwise to every order, the differentiated series converging uniformly on $K$; in particular the potential is $C^\infty$ on $\{|x|>a\}$.

(c) **Ball boundary branch.** For $f\in L^2(S^2)$ with coefficients $f_{lm}$ the series $u(rn)=\sum_{l,m}r^lf_{lm}Y_{lm}(n)$ converges in $L^2(S^2)$ as $r\uparrow1$ and, with all derivatives, uniformly on each closed ball of radius $<1$, is harmonic on the open unit ball, and is the unique harmonic function there with a finite $\sup_{r<1}\|u(r\cdot)\|_2$ and $L^2$ boundary limit $f$; for continuous $f$ it equals the Poisson integral $(1-r^2)/(4\pi|rn-n'|^3)$ of $f$ and extends continuously to the closed ball with boundary values $f$.

This is a statement about the Newtonian integral of a compactly supported $L^1$ density and about harmonic functions; no physical charge distribution or electrostatic interpretation is asserted. In every coefficient integral the factor $|y|^lY_{lm}(y/|y|)$ is defined at $y=0$ by its homogeneous polynomial extension: zero for $l\ge1$ and the constant degree-zero harmonic for $l=0$. This is a finite assignment, and changing its value at that null singleton changes no integral.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mathcal P_l$ denote the real vector space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $l$ on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-homogeneous-polynomial-and-homogeneous-ideal]], [[def-monomials-multidegree-and-total-degree]]), $H_l=\ker(\Delta:\mathcal P_l\to\mathcal P_{l-2})$ with $\mathcal P_k=\{0\}$ for $k<0$, and let spherical harmonics of degree $l$ be the restrictions of $H_l$ to $S^2$, with unnormalised surface measure $d\Omega$ of total mass $4\pi$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]). Then $\mathcal P_l=H_l\oplus|x|^2\mathcal P_{l-2}$, $\dim H_l=2l+1$, harmonics of distinct degree are orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$, and the union over $l$ of the spaces of spherical harmonics admits a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). For any real orthonormal basis $Y_{lm}$, $m=1,\dots,2l+1$, of degree-$l$ harmonics the addition theorem holds:

$$\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')=\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}P_l(n\cdot n'),$$

where $P_l$ is the Legendre polynomial of the convergent zonal kernel lemma ([[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]). The Laplacian is the Euclidean one ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). This supplies the harmonic decomposition, orthogonality, completeness and exact addition kernel; it does not assert higher boundary regularity. The purely polynomial decomposition and finite dimension identities use no Choice; the surface/$L^2$/completeness claims retain the stated Countable Choice.

For $z\in[-1,1]$ define the real polynomial $P_l(z)=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi\bigl[z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\,\cos\theta\bigr]^l\,d\theta$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$. Then $P_l$ is a real polynomial of degree at most $l$ with $|P_l(z)|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, $P_l(1)=1$, and for $|q|<1$ the series $\sum_{l\ge0}q^lP_l(z)$ converges absolutely and uniformly on $[-1,1]$ with

$$(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}=\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}q^lP_l(z),$$

where the branch is the analytic square root equal to $1$ at $q=0$ ([[def-series-of-real-functions]], [[thm-weierstrass-m-test-for-function-series]]). Consequently, for $x\ne0$, $r:=|x|>|y|$ and $n=x/|x|$ and $N\in\mathbb N_0$,

$$\bigl|\,|x-y|^{-1}-\sum_{l=0}^{N}|y|^l|x|^{-l-1}P_l(n\cdot y/|y|)\bigr|\le|y|^{N+1}|x|^{-N-2}(1-|y|/|x|)^{-1},$$

uniformly on $|y|\le a<r$ (with $y=0$ interpreted by the zero higher terms), and after integrating against an $L^1$ source the corresponding multipole expansion converges with that error times its $L^1$ norm. For the integrated $L^1$-source and every-spatial-derivative assertions, assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) through the Lebesgue and harmonic-estimate interfaces. On an observation compact set disjoint from $\overline{B_a(0)}$ every fixed spatial derivative series converges uniformly, uniformly also over $|y|\le a$, by harmonicity of the coefficient terms and [[thm-interior-derivative-estimates-for-harmonic-functions]]. The initial finite-Riemann polynomial/generating assertions are choice-free. This lemma supplies the convergent zonal kernel; it does not by itself prove a spherical $L^2$ basis or boundary convergence.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $f$ have derivatives through order $n$ at $a$, and let $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical embedding. The **Taylor polynomial of degree at most $n$ about $a$** is
$$T_{n,a}f(x):=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(j)}(a)}{\iota(j!)}(x-a)^j.$$
The **Taylor remainder** is $R_{n,a}f(x):=f(x)-T_{n,a}f(x)$.

The factorials are natural numbers as in [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]] and enter real arithmetic only through $\iota$ ([[def-canonical-natural]]); they are nonzero ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]). The sum and powers are those of [[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]], and [[def-integer-power]]. For $n=0$, $T_{0,a}f$ is the constant $f(a)$.

For $0\le r\le n$,
$$(T_{n,a}f)^{(r)}(x)=\sum_{j=r}^{n}\frac{f^{(j)}(a)}{\iota((j-r)!)}(x-a)^{j-r}.$$
Consequently $(T_{n,a}f)^{(r)}(a)=f^{(r)}(a)$, and $R_{n,a}f$ and its derivatives through order $n$ vanish at $a$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and suppose $f$ has derivatives through order $n+1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$, with the usual endpoint continuity. If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ throughout that interval, then
$$|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le \frac{M}{\iota((n+1)!)}|x-a|^{n+1}.$$

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $f\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ with harmonic coefficients $f_{lm}$ in an orthonormal basis of the spherical-harmonic lemma ([[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]]), and for $0\le r<1$ set $u(rn)=\sum_{l,m}r^lf_{lm}Y_{lm}(n)$ (the $l=0$ term being the constant value at $r=0$). Then the series and all its derivatives converge uniformly on every closed smaller ball, $u$ is harmonic there ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]), $u(r\,\cdot)\to f$ in $L^2(S^2)$ as $r\uparrow1$, and $u$ is the unique harmonic function on the unit ball with $\sup_{r<1}\|u(r\,\cdot)\|_{L^2}<\infty$ and $L^2$ boundary limit $f$. For continuous $f$ the same function is

$$u(rn)=\int_{S^2}\frac{1-r^2}{4\pi|rn-n'|^3}f(n')\,d\Omega(n'),$$

it extends continuously to the closed ball with boundary value $f$, and the kernel is positive of total mass one. This is the stated ball boundary branch; generic smooth-domain classical regularity remains a separate obligation.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f,g\in L^1(\mu)$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $f=g$ almost everywhere;
2. for every measurable $A$,
   $$\int_A f\,d\mu=\int_A g\,d\mu.$$

For integrable real or complex $h$, the notation in condition 2 means
$\int_A h\,d\mu:=\int h\chi_A\,d\mu$; the product is integrable because
$|h\chi_A|\le|h|$.

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $\phi:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Then $\nabla\phi$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}\nabla\phi=0\qquad\text{on }U.$$

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. (a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let $\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative $\partial_t$ at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], $$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$ (b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on $I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]])

derivations.claim: Establish the absolute convergence of the coefficients and the null-singleton convention. On $S^2$ the diagonal addition theorem gives $\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)^2=(2l+1)/(4\pi)$ [F8], so $|Y_{lm}(n)|\le((2l+1)/(4\pi))^{1/2}$ for every $n$; for $\lambda_3$-a.e. $y$ with $\rho(y)\ne0$ one has $y\in\overline B_a(0)$ and $|y|\le a$ [F13], so the integrand of $q_{lm}$ is dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by $a^l((2l+1)/(4\pi))^{1/2}|\rho|\in L^1$, and $q_{lm}$ is absolutely convergent by [F12]; the definition at $y=0$ affects a null singleton only and changes no integral by [F12].

Prove the exterior expansion and its tail bound (a). By [F3] and [F2] the potential satisfies $\varphi(x)=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho(x)=(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(y)|x-y|^{-1}\,d\lambda_3(y)$ for $r>a$, and [F7] gives $\int\rho(y)|x-y|^{-1}dy=\sum_{l,m}\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}\frac{Y_{lm}(n)}{r^{l+1}}\int|y|^lY_{lm}(y/|y|)\rho\,dy$ with absolute and uniform convergence on $\{|x|\ge r_0\}$ for every $r_0>a$ and the stated tail bound; multiplying the identity and its tail bound by the finite positive constant $(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ [F4] and using scaling [F12] gives (a), with the coefficients exactly the $q_{lm}$ of step 1.1.

Identify the degree-zero and degree-one terms and the exterior remainder, proving the first part of (b). By [F7] the degree-zero and degree-one terms of the parenthesised series are the Coulomb and dipole terms with the explicit remainder bound of [[lem-em-coulomb-dipole-remainder]], namely $Q/r+p\cdot x/r^3$ with $|R_0(x)|\le16a^2\|\rho\|_1/r^3$ for $r\ge2a$; scaling by $(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ as in step 2.1 turns the degree-zero term into $Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r)$, the degree-one term into $p\cdot x/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3)$, and the remainder bound into the bound of [[pthm-em-electric-dipole-expansion]] (a), which is therefore reproduced.

Identify the degree-two term with the traceless quadrupole, completing (b). Apply the addition theorem [F8] at $l=2$: $\sum_{m=1}^{5}Y_{2m}(n)Y_{2m}(y/|y|)=\frac{5}{4\pi}P_2(n\cdot y/|y|)$, so by finite linearity [F12] $\sum_{m=1}^5Y_{2m}(n)q_{2m}=\frac{5}{4\pi}\int|y|^2P_2(n\cdot y/|y|)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)$. By [F9] the generating identity $(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}=\sum_lq^lP_l(z)$ holds, and the bound $|P_l(z)|\le1$ in [F9] gives a tail after degree two of modulus at most $|q|^3/(1-|q|)=o(q^2)$ as real $q\to0$. Thus the degree-two partial sum is the Taylor polynomial of the generating function; by [F10] its coefficient of $q^2$ is both $P_2(z)$ and, by the chain rule applied to the power function, $\frac12\frac{d^2}{dq^2}(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}\big|_{q=0}=\frac{3z^2-1}{2}$; hence $P_2(z)=(3z^2-1)/2$ and $|y|^2P_2(n\cdot y/|y|)=(3(n\cdot y)^2-|y|^2)/2$ wherever $y\ne0$. Therefore $\sum_mY_{2m}(n)q_{2m}=\frac{5}{8\pi}\int(3(n\cdot y)^2-|y|^2)\rho\,d\lambda_3=\frac{5}{8\pi}n_iQ_{ij}n_j$ by [F1] and [F12], and the degree-two term of (a) is $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\frac{4\pi}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{r^3}\cdot\frac{5}{8\pi}n_iQ_{ij}n_j=\frac{n_iQ_{ij}n_j}{8\pi\varepsilon_0r^3}$.

Prove the regularity and termwise differentiation (c). By [F7] the series may be differentiated termwise to every order with uniform convergence on every compact $K$ with $\inf_K|x|>a$, and the potential is $C^\infty$ on $\{|x|>a\}$; scaling by the constant $(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ preserves termwise differentiation and uniform convergence [F4, F12]. The field $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ of [F6] is therefore the termwise gradient $-\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\sum_{l,m}\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}\nabla_x(Y_{lm}(n)r^{-l-1})q_{lm}$ on $\{|x|>a\}$, with the same uniform convergence on compact subsets.

Record the scope of the exterior clauses (d). Steps 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 and 5.1 used only the real $L^1$ density vanishing $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$, the region $r>a$ (with the quantitative bounds on $r\ge r_0>a$ and $r\ge2a$), and the framework constants [F4]; no claim on or inside $\overline B_a(0)$, no convergence at $r=a$ and no point-source or empirical assertion was made, and the potential is the fixed-time reading of the static source through [F5].

Prove the ball boundary branch (e). Write $g(un):=\sum_{l,m}u^lf_{lm}Y_{lm}(n)$ for $u\in[0,1)$ and $n\in S^2$ as in [F11] with $u=r/R$ and $n=x/|x|$; then $\varphi_f(rn)=g((r/R)n)$ is smooth and harmonic on $|x|<R$, its series and every derivative converge uniformly on every smaller closed ball because the substitution $x=Rz$ multiplies a derivative of order $\alpha$ by the finite factor $R^{-|\alpha|}$, and the bounds $\sup_{0\le t<1}\|\varphi_f(Rt\,\cdot)\|_2=\sup_{t<1}\|g(t\,\cdot)\|_2\le\|f\|_2$ and $\varphi_f(Rt\,\cdot)\to f$ in $L^2(S^2)$ as $t\uparrow1$ are exactly [F11] in the unit variable; the uniqueness statement carries over because any competitor $v$ on $|x|<R$ gives the competitor $u(z):=v(Rz)$ on the unit ball with the same finite radial $L^2$ bound and boundary limit, so [F11] forces $u=g$ and hence $v=\varphi_f$. For continuous $f$ the Poisson integral of [F11] with $r=|x|/R$ is the displayed formula, and the kernel is positive of mass one. Finally, define $E_f:=-\nabla\varphi_f$, $B:=0$, $\rho:=J:=0$ and time-independent fields on the open ball; then $\varphi_f$ is $C^\infty$, so $E_f$ is a $C^1$ field and $B,\rho,J$ are continuous, and [F14] gives $\operatorname{div}E_f=-\Delta\varphi_f=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E_f=-\operatorname{curl}\nabla\varphi_f=0$, while $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$; all four adopted smooth vacuum Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] hold pointwise with vanishing sources and time derivatives, so this is a full source-free electrostatic Maxwell model inside the ball. No boundary trace for the exterior density and no derivative boundary regularity for arbitrary $f$ is used or claimed.

Assemble the theorem and close. Step 2.1 gives (a), steps 3.1 and 4.1 give (b), step 5.1 gives (c), step 6.1 records the scope (d), and step 7.1 gives the independent ball boundary branch (e) with its source-free Maxwell completion; the only nonconstructive assumptions are the declared Countable Choice inherited from the Lebesgue, spherical-harmonic and ball-series interfaces, and no exterior trace, singular-source expansion or empirical content is asserted.

citations.quote: For the Lebesgue branches (a) and (b) assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the exact measure interface ([[def-countable-choice]]); the finite sums in branch (c) are defined and computed without Choice. Let the laboratory region, its chart, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\delta_{ij}$ be the Kronecker symbol in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame, with $|y|$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This definition assigns **source moments** to a static charge distribution in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (d) and (e). Three branches are declared. (a) [Absolutely continuous branch] Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and vanish $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $\overline B_a(0)=\{y:|y|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The **total charge** $Q$, the **dipole moment** $p$, the **degree-$l$ Cartesian moments** $M_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and the **traceless quadrupole** $Q_{ij}$ are $$Q:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p_i:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_i\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\ (l\ge1),$$ $$M^{(0)}:=Q,\qquad M_i:=p_i,\qquad Q_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$ with $l\ge1$ and indices in $\{1,2,3\}$; units are C for $Q$, C m for $p$, C m$^l$ for the degree-$l$ Cartesian moment and C m$^2$ for $Q_{ij}$, and all integrals are in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. The **total charge** $Q$, the **dipole moment** $p$, the **degree-$l$ Cartesian moments** $M_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and the **traceless quadrupole** $Q_{ij}$ are $$Q:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p_i:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_i\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\ (l\ge1),$$ $$M^{(0)}:=Q,\qquad M_i:=p_i,\qquad Q_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$ with $l\ge1$ and indices in $\{1,2,3\}$; units are C for $Q$, C m for $p$, C m$^l$ for the degree-$l$ Cartesian moment and C m$^2$ for $Q_{ij}$, and all integrals are in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Each integral is absolutely convergent: since $\rho=0$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$, and the maps $y\mapsto y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}$ and $y\mapsto 3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}$ are bounded $\lambda_3$-a.e. on that ball by $a^l$ and by $4a^2$ respectively, the integrands are dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by $a^l|\rho|$ and $4a^2|\rho|$, which lie in $L^1$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). The traceless quadrupole is traceless, $$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$ because $\sum_{i=1}^3(3y_i^2-|y|^2)=0$ pointwise, and summing the three integrable functions $3y_i^2\rho-|y|^2\rho$ and applying finite linearity of the integral on $L^1$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]) evaluates the sum as the integral of the pointwise-zero function; replacing $\rho$ by an equal $\lambda_3$-a.e. density changes no moment ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). (b) [General locally integrable branch] If instead $\rho\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ is real and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^l|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)<\infty$ for a given integer $l\ge0$, then the degree-$l$ Cartesian moments of the same formula are absolutely convergent and defined; if the absolute weighted moment $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^L|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)$ is finite for some real $L\ge0$, then every integer Cartesian degree $0\le l\le L$ is defined, and in particular $Q=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3$ is absolutely convergent, so that $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ is a conclusion of this branch and not an added hypothesis. Here $\rho$ is restricted to the closed unit ball, where it is integrable by local integrability, and outside it $|y|^l\le|y|^L$; splitting the nonnegative integral over these two measurable sets and applying monotonicity and additivity of the integral gives $\int|y|^l|\rho|\le\int_{\overline B_1(0)}|\rho|+\int_{\{|y|>1\}}|y|^L|\rho|<\infty$ ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-metric-ball]]). The convention $|y|^0=1$ includes the origin, no compact support and no $L^1$-membership is assumed in this branch, and Cartesian monomials of degree $l$ have modulus at most $|y|^l$, so all lower moments, including $Q$, exist together with the degree-$l$ moment. (c) [Finite system of stationary point charges] Let $N\ge0$, let $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\mathbb R^3$ and let $q_1,\dots,q_N\in\mathbb R$ be charge parameters ([[def-em-sources]] (a)), read as the stationary point charges $q_k\delta_{x_k}$ in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e); for $N=0$ the lists are empty and every sum below is the empty sum $0$. Define $$Q:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k,\qquad p:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_kx_k,\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\,x_{k,i_1}\cdots x_{k,i_l}\ (l\ge1),\qquad M^{(0)}:=Q,$$ $$Q_{ij}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\bigl(3x_{k,i}x_{k,j}-|x_k|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr),$$ finite sums in the sense of [[def-finite-sum]] ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]); again $$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$ by finite distributivity

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units, constants and symbols of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and let $(\rho,J)$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$, all of class $C^1$ (with every additional derivative appearing below existing and continuous); $\partial_t$ is the partial time derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. (a) [Static regime] The **static (time-independent) electromagnetic regime** on $\Omega\times I$ is the requirement $$\partial_tE=0,\qquad\partial_tB=0,\qquad\partial_t\rho=0,\qquad\partial_tJ=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$ (b) [Pure electrostatics] The **pure electrostatic regime** is the static regime together with $J=0$ and $B=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. (c) [Reduced equations] If the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds in the static regime, then the four Maxwell equations reduce to $$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied at each fixed time; in the pure electrostatic regime the reduction is exactly the pair $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$. (d) [Fixed-time reading] In the static regime $E,B,\rho,J$ do not depend on $t$, so each is the pullback along $(y,t)\mapsto y$ of a single map on $\Omega$; this fixed-time reading (the spatial field or source) is the object analysed by the electrostatic statements of this page, and no other time dependence is introduced. The equations of (c) are equations between those spatial maps. (e) [Static-to-distributional reading] Let fields $E,B$ and volume densities $\rho,J$ be locally integrable and time independent on $\Omega\times I$, and let $\Omega$ be open. Then, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the cited measure and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]), the weak equations of the solution predicate of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e) for these time-independent objects hold if and only if the four spatial equations $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$; the passage between them is the integration in $t$ of the pairings against $C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ tests, justified by [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] after identifying fields and densities with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). In particular a **stationary point charge** at $x_0\in\Omega$ with charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ is the point source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with constant trajectory $z(t)\equiv x_0$, whose pairing is $\psi\mapsto q\int_I\psi(x_0,t)\,dt$ and whose fixed-time reading is the spatial point source $\eta\mapsto q\eta(x_0)$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]])

Its positive and negative parts are $$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$ they are measurable by [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.
